                                                                       Summary of Responsive Testimony
                                                                                     of Frank J. Beling

                          Summary of the Responsive Testimony of Frank J. Beling
                      on Behalf of Gentner F. Drummond, Oklahoma Attorney General

                Mr. Frank J. Beling submitted pre-filed responsive testimony in the present Case on August

         5, 2026. Mr. Beling summarized his educational and professional experience before addressing

         Oklahoma Gas and Electric Company’s (“OG&E” or “Company”) request for Commission

         Approval of Electric Service Agreements and Preapproval of Capacity Purchase Agreements

         (“CPAs”) pursuant to 17 O.S. § 286(C).

         Summary of Recommendations

                Mr. Beling first discussed the Company’s forecasted need for additional capacity. Mr.

         Beling explained that new large loads are a significant driver of that need, and that Google’s

         projected load represents a meaningful portion of the Company’s projected demand forecast. Mr.

         Beling also described the Company’s recent resource procurement efforts and explained that

         Google secured and sold to the Company two CPAs to help address the capacity need associated

         with Google’s proposed data center load.

                Next, Mr. Beling discussed the Company’s requested preapproval of cost recovery for the

         Rush Springs and High Spring CPAs. Mr. Beling also explained that the CPAs were not bid into

         the Company’s 2024 All-Source Request for Proposals (“RFP”) but instead resulted from

         negotiations between the Company and Google after the RFP process. Mr. Beling noted that the

         CPAs appear to have favorable pricing compared to the CPA options available in the Company’s

         RFP, but Mr. Beling also elaborated that the Company did not evaluate the CPAs using the same

         scoring methodology applied to the RFP bids. Mr. Beling then recommend that in the future the

         Company evaluate post-RFP proposals using the same scoring methodology applied in the

         applicable competitive solicitation when those proposals are relied upon to support a request for

         pre-approval of cost recovery.      Mr. Beling noted that the Attorney General continues to

         recommend resources be evaluated in an RFP process. However, based on the particular facts and

         circumstances in this Case, the Attorney General does not object to the selection of the two CPAs.

                Subsequently, Mr. Beling summarized the provisions of the Company’s proposed Electric

         Service Agreements with Google, including the proposed Supplemental Resource Administrative

         Charge. Mr. Beling explained that one of the purposes of this charge is to provide the Company

         with a mechanism for earning a return. Mr. Beling stated that although he generally does not

         support a utility earning a return on CPAs, Mr. Beling explained the Supplemental Resource

         Administrative Charge is acceptable in this Case because it is related to the unique set of

         transactions between Google and the Company and does not affect other customers’ rates. Mr.

         Beling further clarified that any approval of the Supplemental Resource Administrative charge

         should not be viewed as precedent for allowing utilities to earn a return on CPAs.

                Next, Mr. Beling discussed several risks associated with serving large loads such as

         stranded investment, cost shifts due to lagging allocation factors, misallocation of Construction

         Work in Progress, and upward rate pressure on Company rates. For each of these risks, Mr. Beling

         discussed if the risks are addressed by the terms of the ESAs.

                Mr. Beling then addressed the Company’s assertion that adding Google’s load will result

         in reduced rates for the other classes. Mr. Beling described the analysis performed by the Company

         to reach this conclusion, and explained how it fails to appropriately recognize the costs associated

         with serving Google.

                Next, Mr. Beling discussed the “failsafe” analysis proposed by the Company. Mr. Beling

        explained that such a mechanism is a beneficial tool to identify any adverse rate impacts caused by

                                                                        Summary of Responsive Testimony

        Google. Mr. Beling described how the Company did not provide details on the methodology that

        should be used in the analysis, and Mr. Beling explained how the analysis should be performed.

                Afterward, Mr. Beling discussed additional consumer protections that should apply to the

         Company’s service to Google and other new large load customers. Mr. Beling recommend that if

         future network transmission upgrades are required to serve Google’s load, Google should pre-fund

         the portion of those costs necessary to prevent an increase in transmission related costs allocated

         to other customer classes. Mr. Beling also recommend that the Company update allocation factors

         on a more frequent basis, and that the Company should develop a mechanism to ensure that new

         large load customers participate in their fair share of any approved return on Construction Work

         in Progress (“CWIP”).

                Finally, Mr. Beling discussed the interaction between the ESAs and any future large load

         tariff. Mr. Beling explained that while the rates in the ESAs are subject to change according to a

         subsequent tariff, many of the non-rate terms and conditions of the ESAs would remain in effect.

         Mr. Beling then compared the protections in the ESAs with protections in the Company’s proposed

         large load tariff. Mr. Beling noted that although the Attorney General’s preference is that the

         special contracts provide protections at least as stringent to those included in the new large load

         tariff once approved, the proposed special contracts comply with HB 2992.
